I'm trying to plant on an area that's very wet. The soil is heavy and thick with clay, and all last spring I found standing water in low areas. Earlier attempts to plant in this area quickly failed, because roots couldn't get into the soil and plants couldn't get regular moisture.

I'm building a drainage field to solve this. I have no idea what I'm doing - we'll see how it goes.

I started by reading about Hügelkultur style composting and eyeing up an old brushpile which was too wet to burn. I didn't want to make a big pile, but just a simple flat square to plant on. I dug into the brushpile and sticks in the center were already showing signs of decomposition - that's a good sign!

I layered sticks over the grass, breaking them up as I went. The biggest sticks went on the bottom layer and I built it up to about four inches thick before starting on the next bit. I spread a bale of straw, then horse manure, then straw again to make a sandwich of planting media to rest on top.

I still need to spread a final layer of pulverized soil on top. The plan is that after settling over the winter I'll have a floating mat of rich soil over a high-drainage grid of sticks. As this decomposes I hope to end up with a porous soil structure that's got all kinds of good bacteria and fungus in it.

I've got another equal amount of horse manure and straw that I'll till into the soil, that way I can compare the drainage pile's performance against a more traditional gardening method. Here's the overall garden, still in need of topsoil and tiller.

Will it turn out that way? Who knows. We'll find out once winter ends and I can start planting in this stuff.
